items.title: Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns
items.summary: Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.
items.body: Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult. Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials. Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance. Devon Energy ( DVN ), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

items.title: Centrica boss says he is 'hugely concerned' over impact of soaring energy bills
items.summary: Chris O'Shea says the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills will increase when prices jump in the new year.
items.body: The boss of British Gas owner Centrica says he is "hugely concerned" about the impact the expected jump in energy bills in January will have on consumers. Chris O'Shea told the BBC he thought the number of people unable or unwilling to pay their energy bills would rise when prices go up in the new year. The new energy price cap to take effect from January will be announced on Wednesday and consultancy Cornwall Insight has forecast it will jump by £443 a year for a typical household. The government has said some households will get £100 to help with energy bills, but Citizens Advice said it was a "drop in the ocean" while one pressure group called for action on "inflated energy firm profits".

items.title: UK-EU food deal hailed by British firms: ‘We’re pretty aligned anyway’
items.summary: Exporters welcome end in sight for Brexit checks – but are frustrated that implementation will take so long British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products. The…
items.body: British producers have broadly welcomed the UK’s deal with the EU, designed to remove the vast majority of physical checks on food, plants and animal products. The sanitary and phytosanitary (SPS) deal is expected to benefit Britain’s food exporters and will enable UK delicatessens and other small retailers to import European cheese and wine again, something that became economically unviable because of costly Brexit checks. The agreement is due to take effect on 1 March 2028 and is also intended to reopen the EU market for UK products including fresh sausages, burgers, seed potatoes and molluscs. However, several years after the UK left the bloc, upending many decades-old trading arrangements, some food exporters said they would remain cautious until the deal came into force.

items.title: The Nasdaq is in freefall. Here's one stock to look at
items.summary: Elevated options premiums are creating an opportunity in Amazon
items.body: I asked Claude after Friday's close what I should do about the tanking stock market. Its advice was surprisingly useful: avoid panic selling and look for opportunities. A 40 VIX , which it touched Friday, might provide those opportunities. Specifically, a higher VIX (higher options premiums) signals fear, but it also creates an opportunity to sell elevated premium in some premium stocks, like Amazon . Amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. Trailing 12-month operating cash flow rose 29% to $168.3 billion. However, infrastructure investment accelerated, resulting in more than $42 billion in negative cash flow. The competing forces of accelerating growth and the cost of supplying it could keep the stock in its range over the next four weeks.

items.title: Employers are being asked to give interview feedback - here's what applicants want
items.summary: People say they often hear nothing back after applying for jobs. But could employers be forced to respond to every applicant?
items.body: Have you ever applied for a job or attended an interview, only to hear absolutely nothing back from the employer? So-called "job ghosting" has become a big problem for jobseekers in the UK, leaving them "demoralised", denting their confidence and undermining their hopes of finding work. It's an issue that was mentioned in former minister Alan Milburn's major review into young people who are not in employment, education or training - those dubbed as Neets - this week. Among his recommendations - aimed at reducing the proportion of Neets from 13% to about 5% by 2036 - Milburn proposed that large employers should give all unsuccessful job applicants under 25 "meaningful feedback". The report's proposals relate mostly to England, with a recommendation that Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland adapt the principles to suit their own systems.

JLR launched legal action over the seven-seater Ti7 SUV earlier this year after BYD announced on its website that it was taking orders from UK customers for the vehicle. Earlier this month, bailiffs acting for JLR were reported to have seized digital records from BYD’s offices . “In these summary proceedings, the preliminary relief judge rules that ​the Ti7 infringes the EU design of Jaguar Land Rover ,” said the ruling from the district court in The Hague.

items.title: Quantum computing’s first real-world payoff may come in energy, not drug discovery
items.summary: Quantum computing firms are testing energy-grid optimization, solar materials and hydrogen catalysts as they pursue practical uses.
items.body: For years, the case for quantum computing has rested on ambitious promises, from discovering new drugs by simulating how molecules behave to optimizing supply chains and airline schedules. Many of the biggest aims are still likely to be years, if not decades, away. But quantum software, which uses algorithms designed to solve complex problems faster than conventional computers, is already being tested on a more immediate challenge: the energy transition, from keeping power grids stable to finding better materials for solar cells and hydrogen production. Phasecraft, a quantum software company founded in Bristol, England, in 2019, is one of the firms putting the technology to work in energy. It raised $34 million in Series B funding in 2025, and in September this year announced plans to set up U.S. headquarters in Arlington, Virginia .

items.title: Italian jeweller and businessman Paolo Bulgari dies aged 89
items.summary: In a statement to Italian media, his family remember him as "the greatest jeweller of our time".
items.body: Italian jeweller Paolo Bulgari, who helped turn his family's business into a global luxury brand, has died in Rome aged age 89. His family announced the news, remembering him as "the greatest jeweller of our time", according to Italian media. Paolo Bulgari was Chairman of the Bvlgari Group since 1984 and its jewellery pieces have adorned Hollywood stars and royalty including Diana, Princess of Wales. The company Bvlgari posted an online tribute to the "true creative soul", whose work would "continue to inspire generations to come". The firm, Bulgari, was set up by his grandfather, Greek silversmith Sotirios Voulgaris, in Rome in the late 19th century - who later adapted his name to Bulgari in Italian.

items.title: UK taxpayers held more than £1tn in offshore tax havens, latest HMRC data shows
items.summary: Figures show recent 10% rise in total held in financial centres such as Jersey and Panama, raising fears over cost to public purse The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential…
items.body: The amount of money UK taxpayers hold in offshore accounts in tax havens has exceeded £1tn for the first time, raising concerns about potential losses to the public purse. HM Revenue and Customs (HMRC) data, obtained by the TaxWatch thinktank through freedom of information requests, shows between 2022 and 2024 the value of balances held offshore in tax havens increased by 10%. These were the latest available figures. The list of tax havens represented in the HMRC data was based on one originally put together by academics from the EU Tax Observatory , and includes jurisdictions such as Hong Kong, the Isle of Jersey, Switzerland, Liechtenstein and Panama. While much of the money in the offshore accounts will have been correctly declared to the UK’s tax authority, large sums are still proving hard to track down and claw back.

items.body: Employees at Foundation Future Industries were told that their health benefits through administrator Rippling have been terminated, according to a memo obtained by CNBC, adding to mounting signs of financial distress at the humanoid robot startup advised and backed by Eric Trump . Foundation told staff in a Friday evening email that they'd be offered coverage through COBRA, the federal law that generally lets workers temporarily keep their health insurance after losing benefits by paying the full premium out of pocket. "Because our last pay run through Rippling was in October, they have ended our benefits with them retroactive to October," a Foundation human resources manager said in the memo.

items.title: MP criticises Guernsey and Jersey company ownership register plans
items.summary: Sir Andrew Mitchell says access should be easier for people tackling financial crime.
items.body: Plans to improve transparency over company ownership in Guernsey and Jersey have come under criticism from a Westminster MP, who says they "do not go nearly far enough". The comments come after Guernsey , external and Jersey , external set out plans to allow approved applicants access to information about who owns or controls companies when investigating suspected financial crime. Sir Andrew Mitchell, who has campaigned for greater scrutiny of company ownership, said there were "immediate indications" the proposals would fall short. He said limits on access to the information could mean "national security threats may remain entirely invisible to investigators". The plans follow a joint commitment made by Guernsey, Jersey and the Isle of Man in December 2023 to increase transparency around company ownership and help tackle money laundering, terrorist financing and other financial crime.

items.title: The looming UK winter may spawn a double headache for Andy Burnham | Richard Partington
items.summary: ‘Raising growth in every postcode’ has been the PM’s rallying cry but deep regional disparities and rising energy bills pose problems this winter Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year…
items.body: Andy Burnham faces two, related problems: Britain faces deep regional disparities and it is entering the coldest months of the year with rising inflation. Since entering Downing Street, raising “growth in every postcode” has been the prime minister’s rallying cry, as he bids to close the gaping chasm in living standards between the richest and poorest areas of the country. But as the war in the Middle East intensifies, the task of spreading prosperity far and wide has only become more difficult. On Wednesday, the regulator Ofgem is expected to confirm a 26% increase in the energy price cap from January, pushing the annual bill to £2,166 for a typical household. Rising petrol prices and diesel hitting a record high lifted the UK’s headline inflation rate to 3.6% in October , its highest level in a year. The Bank of England says inflation could hit 5% next year.

items.title: Pizza chains are under pressure. GLP-1 use is only one part of the problem
items.summary: Domino's, Papa Johns and Pizza Hut face weaker demand, more delivery competition and changing eating habits, including GLP-1 use.
items.body: Big pizza chains are struggling as weaker consumer spending, a wider variety of dining options and the rise of GLP-1 medications weigh on their sales. The pandemic was a boom time for Domino's Pizza , Papa Johns , Little Caesars and Pizza Hut. But since dining rooms reopened, the biggest U.S. pizza chains have faced an uphill battle to retain their customers. These days, consumers are watching their discretionary spending but have more delivery and takeout options when they do decide to order, thanks to the accessibility of third-party platforms. Plus, food quality and the customer experience have become more important to diners who are looking for value when they order from restaurants. As a result of pizza fatigue and challenges facing the broader restaurant industry, the number of U.S. pizza restaurants has tumbled.

items.title: Revealed: profiles of UK experts on gambling harm being hijacked to push illegal online casinos
items.summary: Findings highlight unscrupulous tactics used by operators in multibillion pound illicit market and challenges facing authorities Prof Heather Wardle has dedicated 20 years to researching the harm caused by gambling. So the University of Glasgow social scientist was horrified to…
items.body: Prof Heather Wardle has dedicated 20 years to researching the harm caused by gambling. So the University of Glasgow social scientist was horrified to learn that her reputation and even her photograph had been hijacked by rogue casinos claiming her endorsement for the very games whose addictive properties she has documented. “I would never review these things and promote them to people,” she said. “It’s completely out of kilter with the research I’ve conducted across my entire career.” Wardle is far from alone in being targeted like this, evidence reviewed by the Guardian suggests. At least six prominent academics appear to have had their identities misappropriated by almost 30 casino websites. Most appear to be “affiliates”, businesses that earn commission by directing online traffic towards gambling firms.

items.title: I’ve studied over 200 kids—to avoid raising a people pleaser, ditch 6 parenting habits: It starts in ‘ordinary, well-intentioned moments’
items.summary: Reem Raouda, a conscious parenting coach who's worked with over 200 families, shares six habits worth reconsidering, like treating disagreement as disrespect.
items.body: We all want to raise children who are kind, respectful and considerate. But sometimes, the very behaviors we praise are the ones teaching our children to put themselves last. A child who never complains, always agrees and goes out of their way to make others happy might seem like a parent's dream. But what if they've simply learned that being easy to love means trying to please everyone all the time? As a conscious parenting coach who's worked with over 200 families, I've seen how people pleasing can begin in the most ordinary, well-intentioned moments at home. We love telling our children how easygoing they are, especially when they rarely complain or make demands. But when being easy earns our approval, children may start believing their needs are a burden and their feelings are better kept to themselves.

items.title: Hacks, AI and conspiracy theories: why are we having so many outages?
items.summary: After chaos at airlines, banks and companies from Microsoft to Apple, people have become convinced the world’s systems are under attack Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to…
items.body: Nicole Reindorf’s American Airlines flight was ready for takeoff in Phoenix when the pilot came on the intercom and announced what was to become the longest nationwide aviation shutdown since 9/11 . Reindorf, 70, had seen the headlines hours before about a global Microsoft outage . She immediately suspected the two were linked in some way by AI-related threats – and that she would not get to the wedding of her best friend’s son in California. “I presumed there had been a hack of the aviation system and that it would be down for days,” she said. Instead, flights resumed later that day and Reindorf was able to make the wedding even if she missed that night’s rehearsal dinner. But passengers appeared to be convinced of two things, she said: “That it was a cyber-attack and that we were not going to be told the truth about it.” This was not an isolated view.

items.title: Cloned number plate victims in England and Wales to get new reporting tool
items.summary: Police launch initiative after steep rise in criminals using method to evade detection and avoid paying penalties Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned. Yarwood’s…
items.body: Sandra Yarwood has a file “about 2in thick” of paperwork relating to the 32 driving fines she received this summer after her car’s number plate was cloned. Yarwood’s black Volkswagen Golf did not move from outside her London home while she was on holiday in Canada, but a similar vehicle with a fraudulent copy of her registration racked up penalty notices totalling £2,560 across five London boroughs. Criminals are using cloned plates to evade detection and avoid paying penalties for dangerous or illegal driving. A record 11,400 drivers contacted the DVLA last year after being issued with fines for offences they said they did not recognise or accept responsibility for: most of which are believed to be a result of cloning. The number of complaints was 9% higher than in 2024 and almost double the number recorded in 2018.

items.title: Climate talks stall as countries mull showdown with Saudi Arabia over fossil fuel phaseout
items.summary: New draft text released at Cop31 summit after countries fail to agree on electrification and finance for developing world Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the…
items.body: Climate talks reached a standstill on Saturday night in Turkey as some countries mulled whether to force a showdown with Saudi Arabia and its allies over the global need to phase out fossil fuels. The co-conveners of the Cop31 UN climate summit , Australia’s Chris Bowen and Turkey’s Murat Kurum, held meetings with scores of countries throughout Saturday until late evening as the fortnight-long talks overran without resolution, with countries and campaigners growing increasingly frustrated at the lack of progress. The key sticking points concerned the insistence by a loose coalition of about 130 countries on including a reference to the “transition away from fossil fuels” in the final outcome of the talks, as well as demands by developing countries to bolster their rights to funding from the rich world to help them adapt to the escalating impacts of the climate crisis.

items.body: Howard Lutnick, the beleaguered US commerce secretary and close ally of Donald Trump , is emerging as Democrats’ prime target when the party takes control of Congress in January. Lutnick is resisting calls to resign amid a bipartisan outcry over his role in the scandal at artificial intelligence (AI) company Nvidia and the sale of microchips to China , the US’s principal geopolitical rival in the race for AI supremacy. The 65-year-old billionaire received a vote of confidence from Trump on Friday but faces growing criticism from some Republicans and a chorus of Democrats vowing to investigate his actions and demanding that he testify on Capitol Hill. Among their questions is whether Lutnick compromised national security to make money for his family.

items.title: A truism for our political leaders: until work again involves respect and decent levels of pay, this crisis will continue | John Harris
items.summary: Last week’s Milburn review contained telling phrases, but the core problem is not Neets: it’s what capitalism as we know it has done to employment Everyday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians…
items.body: E veryday pride and contentment. That’s what work should give us. In 15-plus years of speaking to ordinary people and politicians about the UK’s serial woes and crises, one thing has revealed itself to me time and time again: the mess of cant, contradictions and tensions in our national understanding of work. Indeed, the higher up the hierarchies of power and influence any conversation about work goes, the more one vitally important subject seems to fall away: what paid employment actually is or ought to be. All of this is reflective of a very British kind of amnesia. Of course poorly rewarded, unreliable jobs have always been part of our economy – and in the past a focus of fierce social conflict .

items.title: As the real world falls apart, Grand Theft Auto looks more and more appealing | Dave Schilling
items.summary: All these tech outages are a reminder we’re at the mercy of powers beyond our comprehension. At least in GTA we have control This week marked the release of the highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto VI. Millions around the world checked out of their usual…
items.body: T his week marked the release of the highly anticipated video game Grand Theft Auto VI . Millions around the world checked out of their usual responsibilities in order to immerse themselves in a game where you run errands for your girlfriend in between murdering people. I feel completely alone in not caring about GTA VI, as I famously only play video games where you get to be RoboCop – issuing public nuisance citations to graffiti taggers in between murdering people. I’m a man who knows what he likes. GTA VI has been over a decade in the making. The anticipation built to a fever pitch, with gaming enthusiasts practically going feral at the prospect of finally getting to schlep groceries and engage in casual bird-watching after brutally running over a pedestrian with a stolen Porsche. Our collective addiction to virtual mayhem is guaranteed to crash productivity all across the globe.

items.title: Theresa May’s blast from the past calls Tories back to their unhappy place | Peter Walker
items.summary: Conservatives may instinctively want to push back against closer EU ties, but they have to train their focus elsewhere Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been…
items.body: Anyone who accidentally switched to BBC One at about 9.45am on Sunday to be greeted by Theresa May awkwardly espousing the virtues of Brexit could have been forgiven for thinking they had woken up in around 2018 – and not being especially pleased at the idea. This is one of the problems now facing May’s party. For all that it is a reflex action for Conservatives to push back against closer ties with the EU, Andy Burnham’s decision to pursue such a course plunges them back into their own unhappy place. For Tory MPs and activists with a full set of Brexit campaign medals, this risks being especially triggering. May’s repeated attempts to cobble together a departure deal that could unite her party involved repeated humiliations, among them the heaviest ever parliamentary defeat for a British PM, when the Commons rejected her Brexit plan by a majority of 230.

items.summary: Exclusive: Prospect’s Mike Clancy tells Ian Chapman at UKRI that union has ‘lost confidence’ in his leadership A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and…
items.body: A trade union that counts scientists and engineers among its members says it has lost confidence in the leader of the UK’s national funding agency for science and research, citing concerns about plans for major cuts. The letter from Mike Clancy, the general secretary of Prospect, to Ian Chapman, the chief executive of UK Research and Innovation (UKRI), is the latest development in a row over changes in funding for projects and research facilities. “Writing to a CEO in this tone and to this intent is an extraordinary step for this union to have to take,” Clancy wrote.

items.title: Two groups verify mathematician’s claim that Claude helped prove mathematics problem
items.summary: Anthropic’s Levent Alpöge says it took six weeks for him using the AI tool to solve 19th-century Riemann hypothesis A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important…
items.body: A mathematician at Anthropic has said that the San Francisco -based artificial intelligence (AI) company’s software has helped crack one of the most important unsolved problems in mathematics – and experts say the claim checks out. Levent Alpöge, a Turkish American mathematician, on Friday posted a note on his personal website saying that Claude, the AI software, had helped prove the Riemann hypothesis. He says that Claude helped develop a solution to the problem during the course of about six weeks. On Saturday afternoon, two organizations announced that they had independently verified Alpöge’s claim after reviewing the programming language he used to share the solution.

items.title: ‘I don’t blame any woman for being sucked in’: how the wellness industry is cynically exploiting menopause
items.summary: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘Tequila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic…
items.body: Where women see hot flushes and brain fog, pharmaceutical companies see dollar signs. But are products like lion’s mane mushrooms or even magnets for knickers really helping them? Or is it all just a big capitalist con? ‘T equila?” says a woman brightly, proffering a pink plastic shot glass. It’s barely 10.30 on a Saturday morning, and my perimenopause wellness journey is not going entirely as expected. We are standing in a neon-lit London conference centre amid the hubbub of Pause Live , billed as the UK’s biggest annual women’s health and menopause event and essentially a consumer fair for those in midlife. All around me, women are sampling free squirts of menthol lotion (supposed to cool hot flushes) and paper thimblefuls of slightly grainy, sweet latte made with powdered Peruvian maca root instead of coffee.

items.title: Japan's listening bars find a global audience
items.body: TOKYO -- The concept of the listening bar is difficult to define. In many, vinyl records dominate the room, covering the walls from floor to ceiling. In others, countless CDs fill racks upon racks. In some, you will be shushed if you talk over the music. Most have huge speakers, some built by hand. But one thing unites them -- a love of music.
